title: The kernel: system calls, files, memory and programs
subtitle: MS-DOS 4.00 and FreeBSD 15.1, side by side in the source

slides.title: Two very different kernels

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: Real mode: segment:offset, 1 MB, no protection
MSDOS.SYS: shared library behind INT 21h
Any program may rewrite the interrupt vectors
One program runs; TSRs borrow the CPU
8086 assembly; MSDOS.SYS links 55 objects

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: Long mode, paging, ring 0 versus ring 3
Monolithic kernel entered only by syscalls and traps
Entry points set by the kernel (MSR_LSTAR)
Many processes and threads on many CPUs
C, generated syscall tables, loadable modules

slides.notes: Start from the hardware: the 8088 offers no protection, so MS-DOS could not have any. DOS behaves like a library that every program shares, including its data. FreeBSD relies on paging and privilege levels so that the kernel alone controls its entry points. Keep this contrast in mind for every later topic.

slides.title: Address spaces side by side
slides.caption: One real-mode space for everyone versus one map per process
slides.notes: The left side is schematic; SYSINIT decides the exact order of the DOS tables. The right side is exactly what procstat -v prints for a process. Point out that the DOS arena headers live inside the memory they describe, and that INT 21h goes through a vector any program may rewrite, while FreeBSD is entered only through syscalls, exceptions and interrupts whose entry points the kernel sets.

slides.title: INT 21h: save registers, enter DOS, switch stacks
slides.code:
CALL    save_world
        MOV     [SaveDS],DS
        MOV     [SaveBX],BX
        MOV     BX,CS
        MOV     DS,BX
        ASSUME  DS:DOSGROUP
        INC     [INDOS]                 ; Flag that we're in the DOS
⋮
        MOV     BX,CS                   ; no holes here.
        MOV     SS,BX
ASSUME  SS:DOSGROUP

entry   REDISP
        MOV     SP,OFFSET DOSGROUP:AUXSTACK ; Enough stack for interrupts
        STI                             ; stack is in our space now...
callouts: save_world pushes the caller's registers on the caller's stack
INDOS counts calls in progress
SS becomes DOSGROUP; SP the top of AUXSTACK
Interrupts are enabled only after the switch
slides.notes: This is the heart of the dispatcher in DISP.ASM. The caller's frame stays on the caller's stack, and its address is saved in User_SS:User_SP and in the PSP. Only then does DOS switch to its own stack and re-enable interrupts.

slides.title: Three global stacks of 384 bytes
rows: works while a critical error is handled
may wait for a key and issue INT 28h
disk calls that may raise INT 24h
slides.notes: StackSize is 180h bytes in MS_DATA.ASM. Because these stacks are global, a second disk call started from an interrupt handler would overwrite the first one's frames. This is the concrete reason why MS-DOS is not re-entrant.

slides.title: MS-DOS reports errors in the caller's saved carry flag
slides.code:
entry   SYS_RET_OK
        invoke  FETCHI_CHECK            ; TAG checking for FETCHI
        invoke  get_user_stack
        AND     [SI.user_F],NOT f_Carry ; turn off user's carry flag
⋮
entry   SYS_RET_ERR
        XOR     AH,AH                   ; hack to allow for smaller error rets
⋮
        invoke  get_user_stack
        OR      [SI.user_F],f_Carry     ; signal carry to user
        STC                             ; also, signal internal error
DO_RET:
        MOV     [SI.user_AX],AX         ; Really only sets AH
callouts: get_user_stack returns DS:SI pointing at the saved frame
user_F is the FLAGS word pushed by INT 21h
IRET later reloads FLAGS, so the caller sees CF
slides.notes: Every handle-style call ends here. The kernel never touches the live flags; it edits the copy that INT pushed, and IRET makes the edit visible. Keep this slide up while showing the FreeBSD equivalent on the next one.

slides.title: FreeBSD does the same with PSL_C in the trap frame
callouts: Success: clear PSL_C, results in %rax and %rdx
Failure: errno value in %rax, PSL_C set
libsys stub: jb cerror stores errno and returns -1
slides.notes: cpu_set_syscall_retval edits the saved RFLAGS just like SYS_RET_ERR edits the saved FLAGS. The C library then turns carry into errno and -1 in cerror.S. Ask students why both designs return the error in the accumulator.

slides.title: Two ways into the kernel, step by step
slides.caption: INT 21h saves on the caller's stack, then switches to a global DOS stack; syscall switches to a per-thread kernel stack
slides.notes: Read both rows left to right. The CPU step is hardware in both cases: INT pushes FLAGS, CS and IP and jumps through the vector table; syscall jumps to the address the kernel put in MSR_LSTAR. MS-DOS saves the registers on the caller's stack and then moves to AUXSTACK, IOSTACK or DSKSTACK, shared by the whole machine; FreeBSD switches to the thread's own kernel stack first and builds a trap frame there. Both return by editing the carry bit in the saved flags.

slides.title: System call entry compared
slides.notes: Walk the rows top to bottom while pointing at the listings in the notes. The decisive difference is the per-thread kernel stack. Everything else is surprisingly parallel.

slides.title: InDOS, critical errors and INT 28h
bullets: Function 34h returns ES:BX of INDOS; ErrorMode is the byte before
TSRs may call DOS only when both flags are zero
Console waits call SPOOLINT, which issues INT 28h
During INT 28h the interrupted call is on IOSTACK
So an INT 28h handler may use calls above 0Ch
slides.notes: This is the protocol that made background printing and pop-up utilities possible. It is a convention, not a mechanism: nothing enforces it. Exercise 2.5 asks students to reason about exactly these rules.

slides.title: Three levels in both systems
slides.caption: After DUP or dup, two numbers share one open file and one position
slides.notes: Both systems separate the per-process number from the shared open file. That is why dup shares a file position in both. Mention that FreeBSD's initial table has NDFILE = 20 slots, the same historical 20 as FilPerProc.

slides.title: Handles versus descriptors
slides.notes: The dup2 row is a nice example of SMP thinking: FreeBSD never lets another thread see the target descriptor closed. MS-DOS has no other observer, so the simple order is fine. Exercise 2.6 shows that FORCEDUP of a handle onto itself closes it.

slides.title: One read, two kernels
slides.caption: Study case 2.A follows every hop with a source line
slides.notes: Walk down both columns together. MS-DOS has fewer layers and the CPU busy-waits inside the driver and the BIOS; FreeBSD adds the VFS, the buffer cache and GEOM, and the thread sleeps while the disk does DMA and raises an interrupt.

slides.title: The FAT file system, implemented twice
FAT12: two entries in three bytes
slides.caption: The worked example of Study case 2.B: bytes F0 FF FF 03 40 00 FF 0F 00 encode the chain 2 -> 3 -> 4
slides.notes: Entry n starts at byte n*3/2. Even entries take the low 12 bits of the 16-bit word, odd entries the high 12 bits, so two entries share the middle byte. Decode entry 3 with the class: word 0040h at offset 4, odd, shift right 4 bits, 004. MS-DOS does this in MAPCLUSTER and UNPACK; msdosfs encodes the 1.5 with pm_fatmult/pm_fatdiv = 3/2.

slides.title: MS-DOS: unpack a FAT12 entry
slides.code:
CMP     BX,ES:[BP.dpb_max_cluster]
        JA      HURTFAT
        CALL    MAPCLUSTER
ASSUME  DS:NOTHING
        jc      DoContext
        MOV     DI,[DI]
        JNZ     High12                  ; MZ if high 12 bits, go get 'em
⋮
High12:
        SHR     DI,1
        SHR     DI,1
        SHR     DI,1
        SHR     DI,1
Unpack12:
        AND     DI,0FFFH                ; Clears carry
callouts: MAPCLUSTER returns a pointer to byte n*1.5
Zero flag clear means odd entry: use the high 12 bits
Even entry: mask with 0FFFh
slides.notes: Work the example F0 FF FF 03 40 00 FF 0F 00 on the board first. Then show that the assembly does exactly the three steps. Mention the CLUSSPLIT case for entries that straddle two sectors.

slides.title: FreeBSD: the same three steps in C
callouts: getushort is a little-endian 16-bit load
Odd FAT12 entries are shifted right by 4
Reserved values are normalised for all FAT types
slides.notes: Point out the single ampersand on the odd test; it works because FAT12() yields 0 or 1. msdosfs avoids the straddling case by reading the FAT in blocks of three sectors. Same format, entirely different engineering trade-offs.

slides.title: Numbers fixed by the format

stats.label: FAT12 if clusters + 1 < 4086, in both kernels

slides.notes: Both kernels compare the highest cluster number with 4086: 4096-10 in FAT.ASM and CLUST_RSRVD & FAT12_MASK in msdosfs. The three-sector block is why msdosfs needs no split-entry code. Directory entries are 32 bytes in both, but bytes 12-21 were interpreted differently over time.

slides.title: The MS-DOS memory control block
slides.code:
arena   STRUC
arena_signature     DB  ?               ; 4D for valid item, 5A for last item
arena_owner         DW  ?               ; owner of arena item
arena_size          DW  ?               ; size in paragraphs of item
arena_reserved      DB  3 DUP(?)        ; reserved
arena_name          DB  8 DUP(?)        ; owner file name
arena   ENDS
⋮
arena_owner_system  EQU 0               ; free block indication

arena_signature_normal  EQU 4Dh         ; valid signature, not end of arena
arena_signature_end     EQU 5Ah         ; valid signature, last block in arena
callouts: 16 bytes, one paragraph below each block
Owner 0 = free; next = segment + size + 1
First MCB: the word at ES:[BX-2] after function 52h
slides.notes: The arena is a linked list stored inside the memory it manages. A single stray write corrupts it: allocation (48h), and with it EXEC, then fails with error 7 when the walk reaches the bad header. Contrast with vm_map entries, which live in kernel memory behind a lock.

slides.title: EXEC versus fork + execve

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00 EXEC
bullets: One call: load, build PSP, jump
.EXE relocation adds the load segment
Parent frozen inside its INT 21h
Child inherits JFT, environment copy
Exit code read once with 4Dh

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: fork copies the process, copy-on-write
execve maps PT_LOAD segments, no reading
Parent and child run concurrently
fdcopy at fork, close-on-exec at exec
Status per child via wait4

slides.notes: MS-DOS cannot fork: images contain absolute segment values and there is no paging or scheduler. EXEC keeps the parent suspended and resumes it through the INT 22h address when the child exits. vfork is the closest FreeBSD relative of this model.

slides.title: EXEC versus fork + execve, as a timeline
slides.caption: MS-DOS: the whole child lifetime happens inside the parent's INT 21h call; FreeBSD: two processes
slides.notes: Follow the top lane: the parent issues 4Bh and does not run again until $EXIT IRETs to the instruction after its INT 21h; 4Dh then reads the exit code. In the bottom lane fork1 returns twice, pid in the parent and 0 in the child; the child calls execve, which replaces its address space, and exit1 makes it a zombie and wakes the parent in wait4.

slides.title: Starting the child: InDOS = 0 and a far return
slides.code:
CLI
        MOV     BYTE PTR INDOS,0
        ASSUME  SS:NOTHING
        MOV     SS,AX                   ; set up user's stack
        MOV     SP,DI                   ; and SP
        STI
        PUSH    DS                      ; fake long call to entry
        PUSH    SI
        MOV     ES,DX                   ; set up proper seg registers
        MOV     DS,DX
        MOV     AX,BX                   ; set up proper AX
⋮
        RET
callouts: The child's SS:SP and entry point come from the header
DS = ES = PSP segment, AX = drive validity flags
RET jumps to the child; the parent never left INT 21h
slides.notes: This is the only place where DOS clears InDOS without returning to the caller. The parent's frame stays on the parent's stack until reset_environment resumes it. Ask what happens to the parent's registers in the meantime.

slides.title: Device drivers

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: Header: next, attributes, strategy, interrupt, name
Request packet: unit, command, status
DEVIOCALL: far call strategy, then interrupt
NUL device built into MSDOS.SYS

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: struct cdevsw: one function per operation
/dev/null: null_write consumes the uio
Disks go through GEOM and struct bio
Strategy survives: VOP_STRATEGY, d_strategy

slides.notes: The two-step strategy/interrupt interface would allow queuing, which MS-DOS 4.00 never uses. FreeBSD's strategy routines really do queue requests and complete them asynchronously. Show null.c next to the NUL device header in SYSINITVAR.

slides.title: Concurrency

left.heading: MS-DOS 4.00
bullets: One DOS call at a time
CLI/STI around stack switches
EnterCrit stubs are a single RET
The sharer patches them into INT 2Ah calls

right.heading: FreeBSD 15.1
bullets: Many threads in the kernel on many CPUs
mutex: one atomic compare-and-set when free
Spin mutexes disable interrupts per CPU
Locks on fd tables, vnodes, maps

slides.notes: CRIT.ASM shows how cheaply MS-DOS reserved hooks for multitasking. FreeBSD has to lock every shared structure; the fast path of mtx_lock is one atomic instruction. spinlock_enter is the per-CPU, nestable descendant of CLI.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Both kernels report errors by setting the caller's saved carry flag
MS-DOS is not re-entrant: global stacks and state
Same handle model: per-process table, shared open file
Same FAT rules, opposite engineering trade-offs
Protection and processes need hardware MS-DOS never had
slides.notes: Close by returning to the first slide: almost every difference follows from the hardware and the compatibility promises each system made. The similarities come from MS-DOS 2.x borrowing the Unix model. Next module: the shells that run on top of these kernels.
